metadata.summary: This guideline rates initial imaging examinations for adults with vision loss across six clinical presentations, organized by symptom onset, visual-field findings, and suspected anatomic cause. It addresses traumatic orbital injury, orbital infection or inflammation, orbital masses or vascular lesions, retinal structural abnormalities, optic nerve disorders, and sellar or parasellar disease. It also explains how the clinical scenario and suspected lesion location guide the choice of imaging examination.

conditions_covered: Acute vision loss with infection or inflammatory disorder suspected
Chronic or progressive unilateral vision loss with intraorbital mass-like lesion or vascular lesion suspected
Acute vision loss with retinal structural abnormality suspected
Acute or chronic vision loss with optic nerve abnormality suspected
Bitemporal hemianopia or junctional scotoma with sellar or parasellar mass suspected

infection_management.management: Clinical findings and imaging help distinguish periorbital from postseptal disease and determine whether inpatient IV antibiotics are needed. Imaging also assesses disease extent and complications.
Imaging can identify abscesses that require urgent surgical intervention.

infection_management.pathogen_or_syndrome: Bacterial infection of the paranasal sinuses

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with orbital fractures following trauma.
decision_rules: Most orbital fractures can be repaired after acute swelling resolves; findings such as trapdoor fractures or orbital compartment syndrome may call for more urgent intervention.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The document does not specify a repair technique.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with traumatic optic neuropathy and bone fragment impingement on the optic nerve, hematoma within the optic canal, or an enlarging retrobulbar hematoma accompanied by proptosis.
decision_rules: Emergent surgery is generally reserved for the listed findings rather than performed for traumatic optic neuropathy in general.

recommended_regimens.name: emergent surgical intervention
recommended_regimens.summary: Surgery is generally undertaken emergently when a bone fragment impinges on the nerve, a hematoma is present within the canal, or a retrobulbar hematoma is expanding with proptosis.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Rapid recognition permits timely intervention when needed; the document does not specify a surgical technique.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with severe proptosis and posterior globe tenting after orbital trauma.
decision_rules: Severe proptosis with posterior globe tenting requires emergent orbital decompression to preserve vision.
Establish orbital compartment syndrome from clinical evidence of optic nerve compression; imaging evidence of retrobulbar hemorrhage is not sensitive for its subsequent development.

recommended_regimens.name: emergent orbital decompression
recommended_regimens.summary: Perform urgent decompression when severe proptosis and posterior globe tenting are present.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with orbital infection presenting as cellulitis or associated abscess.
decision_rules: Distinguish periorbital from postseptal disease using clinical findings and imaging to determine whether inpatient IV antibiotics are needed.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The document identifies a potential need for inpatient IV antibiotics but does not specify which patients require them or name an antibiotic regimen. Orbital infection is an ophthalmologic emergency because vision loss and intracranial spread can occur.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with a subperiosteal abscess associated with orbital infection.
decision_rules: A subperiosteal abscess usually calls for surgical drainage.

recommended_regimens.name: surgical drainage
recommended_regimens.summary: Drainage is usually required for a subperiosteal abscess.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients presenting within the designated treatment window.
decision_rules: IV fibrinolytic therapy may be performed within the designated treatment window.
CT head without IV contrast may be obtained before fibrinolysis to exclude intracranial hemorrhage.

alternative_regimens.name: IV fibrinolytic therapy
alternative_regimens.summary: Fibrinolysis may be performed for eligible patients; the document does not specify an agent.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Presentation within the designated treatment window.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The document does not define the treatment window.

decision_rules: Prompt treatment is often necessary to prevent permanent vision loss.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The document does not specify a treatment intervention or regimen.

therapies_index.name: CT maxillofacial without IV contrast
approved_indications: Initial imaging of acute posttraumatic visual defect when orbital injury is suspected, particularly if additional facial injuries may be present.
therapies_index.administration: Imaging without IV contrast; coverage typically extends from above the frontal sinuses through the mandible.

therapies_index.name: CT orbits without IV contrast
approved_indications: Initial imaging of acute posttraumatic visual defect when injury is confined to the orbital region.
May be appropriate as initial imaging for acute vision loss when orbital infection or inflammation is suspected.
therapies_index.administration: Imaging without IV contrast, generally using a field of view centered on the orbits.

therapies_index.name: CT head without IV contrast
approved_indications: May be appropriate alongside orbital or maxillofacial imaging after trauma if traumatic brain injury or intracranial hemorrhage is suspected.
May be performed before IV fibrinolytic therapy for acute central retinal artery occlusion to exclude intracranial hemorrhage.
therapies_index.administration: Imaging without IV contrast.

therapies_index.name: MRI orbits without and with IV contrast
approved_indications: Initial imaging of acute vision loss when orbital infection or inflammation is suspected.
Preferred initial imaging for chronic or progressive unilateral vision loss when an orbital mass or vascular lesion is suspected.
Initial imaging of acute or chronic vision loss when an optic nerve abnormality is suspected.
May be performed after initial diagnosis to investigate a mass or another cause of exudative retinal detachment.
therapies_index.administration: Orbital MRI before and after IV contrast; postcontrast orbital images should use fat suppression.

therapies_index.name: CT maxillofacial with IV contrast
approved_indications: Initial imaging of acute vision loss with suspected orbital infection or inflammation when the suspected source or extent may lie outside the orbital CT field of view.
therapies_index.administration: Maxillofacial CT with IV contrast.

therapies_index.name: CT orbits with IV contrast
approved_indications: Initial imaging of acute vision loss with suspected orbital infection or inflammation when orbital coverage is sufficient.
May be appropriate for chronic or progressive unilateral vision loss with a suspected orbital mass or vascular lesion, including as complementary imaging for calcification or bone involvement.
therapies_index.administration: Orbital CT with IV contrast; dynamic postcontrast imaging is described for characterizing cavernous venous malformation.

therapies_index.name: MRI head without and with IV contrast
approved_indications: May be appropriate when intracranial extension or complications of orbital infection or inflammation are suspected.
May be appropriate to assess intracranial extension of an orbital mass.
May be appropriate alongside orbital MRI when an optic nerve disorder could have intracranial manifestations.
May be appropriate when suspected sellar or parasellar disease is not confined to the sellar region.
therapies_index.administration: Head MRI before and after IV contrast.

therapies_index.name: MRI sella without and with IV contrast
approved_indications: Preferred initial imaging for bitemporal hemianopia or junctional scotoma when a sellar or parasellar mass is suspected.
therapies_index.administration: Thin-section imaging before and after IV contrast, with a small field of view centered on the sellar and suprasellar regions.

therapies_index.name: Arteriography cerebral
approved_indications: May be used to diagnose posttraumatic vascular abnormalities, but is not a first-line examination for posttraumatic vision loss.
May be used to characterize an aneurysm before treatment or during aneurysm treatment, but is not recommended as initial imaging for bitemporal hemianopia or junctional scotoma.

therapies_index.name: MRA head and neck with IV contrast
approved_indications: May be performed subsequently to assess vascular disease in ischemic optic neuropathy; it is not recommended as initial imaging for that presentation.
therapies_index.administration: Head and neck MRA with IV contrast.

therapies_index.name: MRA head and neck without and with IV contrast
approved_indications: May be performed subsequently to assess vascular disease in ischemic optic neuropathy; it is not recommended as initial imaging for that presentation.
therapies_index.administration: Head and neck MRA before and after IV contrast.

therapies_index.name: MRA head and neck without IV contrast
approved_indications: May be performed subsequently to assess vascular disease in ischemic optic neuropathy; it is not recommended as initial imaging for that presentation.
therapies_index.administration: Head and neck MRA without IV contrast.

therapies_index.name: MRA head with IV contrast
approved_indications: May be performed after initial imaging when arterial complications of orbital infection or inflammation are suspected.
MRA may be used after MRI suggests an aneurysm compressing the optic chiasm; this examination is not recommended as initial imaging for bitemporal hemianopia or junctional scotoma.
therapies_index.administration: Head MRA with IV contrast.

therapies_index.name: MRA head without and with IV contrast
approved_indications: MRA may be used after MRI suggests an aneurysm compressing the optic chiasm; this examination is not recommended as initial imaging for bitemporal hemianopia or junctional scotoma.

therapies_index.name: ocular US
approved_indications: May help diagnose acute orbital abnormalities associated with vision loss.
May establish retinal detachment when the posterior eye cannot be assessed by funduscopy, including when vitreous hemorrhage obscures the view.
therapies_index.administration: Usually performed by an ophthalmologist and sometimes by a physician trained in advanced emergency medicine US; it should be avoided when globe rupture is known or suspected.

therapies_index.name: Color Doppler
approved_indications: May be added to ocular US to assess ocular and retinal vascular pathology.

therapies_index.name: Optical coherence tomography
therapies_index.mechanism: Uses near-infrared light waves to produce high-resolution cross-sectional retinal images.
approved_indications: Used by ophthalmologists to evaluate retinal pathology; the document also describes its use in diagnosing optic nerve disorders such as optic neuritis.

therapies_index.name: dilated funduscopic examination
approved_indications: Used with clinical assessment to diagnose retinal detachment.

therapies_index.name: orbital decompression
approved_indications: Emergent intervention for severe proptosis with posterior globe tenting to preserve vision.
therapies_index.administration: Performed emergently in the situation described.

therapies_index.name: surgical drainage
approved_indications: Usually required for a subperiosteal abscess; an orbital abscess detected on imaging may require urgent surgical intervention.

therapies_index.name: IV antibiotics
approved_indications: May be needed as inpatient treatment for postseptal orbital infection; distinguishing postseptal from periorbital disease helps determine this need.
therapies_index.administration: IV administration in an inpatient setting when indicated.

therapies_index.name: IV fibrinolytic therapy
approved_indications: May be performed for central retinal artery occlusion when the patient is within the designated treatment window.
therapies_index.administration: IV administration; the document does not specify a dose or the length of the treatment window.

recommendations.statement: For initial imaging after an acute posttraumatic visual defect with suspected orbital injury, use either CT maxillofacial without IV contrast or CT orbits without IV contrast. Choose the maxillofacial examination when additional facial injuries are suspected; the orbital examination is suited to injury confined to the orbital region.
recommendations.context: Adult; acute posttraumatic visual defect; suspected orbital injury; initial imaging.
recommendations.rationale: These alternative examinations can assess orbital fractures and soft-tissue injuries, but their fields of view differ.

recommendations.statement: Consider CT head without IV contrast as a complementary initial examination when traumatic brain injury or intracranial hemorrhage is suspected alongside facial or orbital trauma.
recommendations.context: Adult; acute posttraumatic visual defect; suspected orbital injury; initial imaging.
recommendations.rationale: A maxillofacial or orbital CT generally does not cover the entire head and brain.

recommendations.statement: For initial imaging of acute vision loss when infection or inflammation is suspected, use MRI orbits without and with IV contrast, CT maxillofacial with IV contrast, or CT orbits with IV contrast. In the emergency setting, contrast-enhanced CT is the first-line examination; select maxillofacial rather than orbital coverage when the suspected process could extend beyond the orbital CT field of view. Orbital MRI can complement CT.
recommendations.context: Adult; acute vision loss; suspected infection or inflammatory disorder; initial imaging.
recommendations.rationale: Contrast-enhanced CT depicts disease extent and abscesses that may require intervention. Orbital MRI provides greater soft-tissue contrast and helps distinguish abscess from phlegmon.

recommendations.source_heading: Variant 2: Adult. Acute vision loss. Infection or inflammatory disorder suspected. Initial imaging.

recommendations.statement: MRI head without and with IV contrast may be used when intracranial spread of suspected orbital infection or inflammation is a concern. CT orbits without IV contrast may be used, although contrast-enhanced CT is preferred for distinguishing an abscess from other inflammatory changes.
recommendations.context: Adult; acute vision loss; suspected infection or inflammatory disorder; initial imaging.
recommendations.rationale: Head MRI can assess intracranial complications. Noncontrast orbital CT can show inflammatory changes, adjacent sinus disease and bone erosion, but is more limited for abscess assessment.

recommendations.statement: Use MRI orbits without and with IV contrast for initial evaluation when chronic or progressive unilateral vision loss raises concern for an intraorbital mass-like or vascular lesion.

The document therefore specifies lower relative radiation level dose-estimate ranges for pediatric examinations than for adult examinations, although its initial-imaging variants address adults.

columns: The ACR Committee on Appropriateness Criteria and its expert panels have developed criteria for determining appropriate imaging examinations for diagnosis and treatment of specified medical condition(s). These criteria are intended to guide radiologists, radiation oncologists and referring physicians in making decisions regarding radiologic imaging and treatment. Generally, the complexity and severity of a patient’s clinical condition should dictate the selection of appropriate imaging procedures or treatments. Only those examinations generally used for evaluation of the patient’s condition are ranked. Other imaging studies necessary to evaluate other co-existent diseases or other medical consequences of this condition are not considered in this document. The availability of equipment or personnel may influence the selection of appropriate imaging procedures or treatments. Imaging techniques classified as investigational by the FDA have not been considered in developing these criteria; however, study of new equipment and applications should be encouraged. The ultimate decision regarding the appropriateness of any specific radiologic examination or treatment must be made by the referring physician and radiologist in light of all the circumstances presented in an individual examination.

conditions.name: Acute posttraumatic visual defect
conditions.description: Visual impairment after trauma when an orbital injury is suspected. Orbital fractures and soft-tissue injuries may threaten vision; the anatomical extent of injury determines whether orbital or broader facial imaging is needed.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Depending on the injury, findings may include diplopia, proptosis, an afferent pupillary defect or vision loss. In patients with associated traumatic brain injury or obtundation, an afferent pupillary defect may be the only clinical indication of traumatic optic neuropathy.

subtypes.name: Orbital fractures
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Fractures may occur alone or alongside midface injuries. Depressed orbital floor fractures may cause diplopia; fractures of the orbital floor >2 cm are more likely to accompany enophthalmos. Lateral or superior wall fractures are associated with greater risk of traumatic optic neuropathy.

subtypes.name: Traumatic optic neuropathy
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Optic canal fractures increase the risk of nerve injury. MRI can show abnormal optic nerve signal, although CT better assesses fractures and displaced bone.

subtypes.name: Orbital compartment syndrome
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Orbital mass effect, including that from retrobulbar hematoma, emphysema or blow-in fractures, may compromise vision. Diagnosis rests on clinical evidence of optic nerve compression rather than detection of hemorrhage on imaging.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify orbital fractures, foreign bodies, globe injury and retrobulbar soft-tissue injury.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Usually Appropriate for initial imaging, particularly after direct blunt or penetrating orbital injury without concern for additional facial fractures.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Its restricted field of view may omit injuries elsewhere in the face.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess orbital injury and additional facial fractures across a broader field of view.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Usually Appropriate for initial imaging when further facial injury is suspected; it is an alternative to CT orbits without IV contrast.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess possible traumatic brain injury, intracranial hemorrhage or skull fracture.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: May Be Appropriate as a complementary initial examination when associated intracranial injury is suspected.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: A head examination may not cover the entire orbits or lower face.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess suspected traumatic optic neuropathy and optic nerve signal changes.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Typically a secondary examination after initial CT; in penetrating injuries, exclude a metallic foreign body first. It is Usually Not Appropriate as initial imaging in this variant.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Optic nerve restricted diffusion lacks sensitivity but is highly specific for traumatic optic neuropathy in the appropriate clinical context.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess selected acute ocular and retrobulbar abnormalities.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Not included in the variant table; avoid when globe rupture is known or suspected.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Assessment of orbital floor fractures is more limited than with CT.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: May identify radio-opaque orbital foreign bodies.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Usually Not Appropriate for initial imaging.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: These examinations are less sensitive than CT for fractures and cannot localize foreign bodies relative to orbital soft tissues as CT can.

long_term_effects: Permanent vision loss may follow an orbital injury or its complications.

conditions.name: Orbital infection
conditions.description: An orbital infection may take the form of cellulitis or a subperiosteal or orbital abscess. Spread from adjacent structures, often infected paranasal sinuses, is a common source. Intracranial spread is possible.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Possible manifestations include local pain and swelling, reduced visual acuity and ophthalmoplegia.

subtypes.name: Periorbital infection
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Distinction from postseptal disease helps determine the need for inpatient IV antibiotics.

subtypes.name: Postseptal infection
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Its identification helps determine the need for inpatient IV antibiotics.

subtypes.name: Subperiosteal abscess
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Usually requires surgical drainage.

subtypes.name: Acute invasive fungal sinusitis
subtypes.distinguishing_features: An aggressive infection associated with high mortality that typically affects immunocompromised patients and can cause orbital complications.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Map orbital infection, distinguish periorbital from postseptal involvement and detect abscess, adjacent sinus disease, bone erosion or superior ophthalmic vein thrombosis.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Usually Appropriate as an initial examination, particularly in the emergency setting when the suspected process fits within the orbital field of view.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The field of view may omit the lower maxillary sinus and maxillary dentition.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess infection or its potential source outside the orbital CT field of view.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Usually Appropriate as an initial alternative to CT orbits with IV contrast when maxillary or dental involvement, or wider facial disease, is suspected.

diagnostic_workup.test: MRI orbits without and with IV contrast
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Define orbital disease and complications and help distinguish abscess from edema, phlegmon, inflammatory disease or a neoplastic lesion.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Usually Appropriate for initial evaluation and complementary to contrast-enhanced CT.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: DWI and postcontrast sequences contribute to distinguishing abscess from other changes.

diagnostic_workup.test: MRI head without and with IV contrast
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess suspected intracranial spread, meningeal involvement or cavernous sinus thrombosis.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: May Be Appropriate alongside or after orbital MRI if intracranial complications are suspected.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Show inflammatory soft-tissue changes, adjacent sinus disease and bone erosion.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: May Be Appropriate initially, although IV contrast is preferred for suspected orbital infection.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Less able than contrast-enhanced CT to distinguish abscess from other inflammatory change.

diagnostic_workup.test: CTA head with IV contrast; CTV head with IV contrast; MRA head without IV contrast; MRV head with IV contrast
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Further investigate suspected arterial or venous complications, including superior ophthalmic vein or cavernous sinus thrombosis.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: These are not supported as first-line examinations in the variant table; vascular concerns may arise from the clinical presentation or initial imaging.

long_term_effects: Permanent vision loss and intracranial complications may occur.

conditions.name: Orbital inflammatory disease
conditions.description: Inflammation of orbital structures may be idiopathic or arise in the setting of granulomatous, inflammatory or autoimmune disease. Imaging and clinical findings may overlap with those of cellulitis or lymphoproliferative lesions.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Manifestations and risk of vision loss depend on the cause and the orbital structures affected.

subtypes.name: Orbital inflammatory syndrome
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Its clinical and imaging features may resemble cellulitis or lymphoproliferative disease.

subtypes.name: Thyroid orbitopathy
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Noncontrast orbital CT can demonstrate extraocular muscle enlargement, lacrimal gland prolapse, increased orbital fat and proptosis.

diagnostic_workup.test: MRI orbits without and with IV contrast
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Characterize orbital inflammation, its extent and complications, and help distinguish it from infection or a mass.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Usually Appropriate for initial imaging.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: DWI and apparent diffusion coefficient values may assist in distinguishing overlapping orbital processes.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess the orbital process, its extent and potential complications.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Usually Appropriate for initial imaging when the suspected process is within the orbital field of view.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess a process extending beyond the orbital CT field of view.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Usually Appropriate for initial imaging when broader facial coverage is needed.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Demonstrate characteristic findings of suspected thyroid orbitopathy.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: May Be Appropriate initially.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: For an abscess, noncontrast CT is more limited than contrast-enhanced imaging.

diagnostic_workup.test: MRI head without and with IV contrast
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Investigate suspected intracranial involvement.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: May Be Appropriate as a complementary examination.

conditions.name: Chronic or progressive unilateral vision loss
conditions.description: This presentation prompts evaluation for an intraorbital mass-like or vascular lesion. Orbital masses can be characterized by their anatomical compartment and may have soft-tissue, osseous or vascular origins.
conditions.epidemiology: Benign orbital masses are more common; malignant tumors become more prevalent in adults older than 60 years of age. Excluding cysts, cavernous venous malformation is the most common benign orbital mass in adults, whereas Non-Hodgkin lymphoma is the most common malignant orbital mass in adults.
conditions.clinical_presentation: A mass or vascular lesion may produce proptosis. Lesions affecting the orbital apex characteristically cause vision loss with ophthalmoplegia.

subtypes.name: Cavernous venous malformation
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Dynamic postcontrast CT can show progressive enhancement.

subtypes.name: Venous varix of the orbit
subtypes.distinguishing_features: CT performed without and with a Valsalva maneuver can establish this diagnosis.

subtypes.name: Non-Hodgkin lymphoma
subtypes.distinguishing_features: The most common malignant orbital mass in adults; FDG-PET/CT can be part of staging after the initial diagnostic evaluation.

subtypes.name: High-flow vascular lesions of the orbit
subtypes.distinguishing_features: A lesion such as arteriovenous malformation may undergo secondary assessment with CTA head.

diagnostic_workup.test: MRI orbits without and with IV contrast
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify and characterize a suspected orbital mass or vascular lesion and define its extent.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Usually Appropriate and the initial imaging examination of choice.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The dedicated orbital protocol depicts orbital compartments at higher resolution than routine head MRI.

diagnostic_workup.test: MRI head without and with IV contrast
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess an orbital mass with possible intracranial extension.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: May Be Appropriate.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Provide complementary assessment of calcification, orbital bone involvement or a primary osseous mass.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: May Be Appropriate; CT may also be a first-line examination if vision loss progresses rapidly.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Cover a large facial mass that secondarily extends into the orbit.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: The variant table rates it Usually Not Appropriate for the specified initial presentation; broader coverage is needed if the mass originates outside the orbit.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Further evaluate a suspected high-flow orbital vascular lesion.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Usually Not Appropriate initially; it may be used in secondary assessment.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify metastatic lesions or contribute to orbital lymphoma staging.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Usually Not Appropriate for initial imaging of this presentation.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: It has limited spatial resolution for small orbital structures, and FDG uptake may overlap between malignancy and benign inflammatory processes.

conditions.name: Retinal detachment
conditions.description: Separation involving the retina can cause acute visual loss. Prompt treatment may be needed to avoid permanent impairment. Diagnosis usually relies on clinical and ophthalmologic examination rather than initial cross-sectional imaging.
conditions.epidemiology: Rhegmatogenous retinal detachment is the most common form.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Acute vision loss may occur. Vitreous hemorrhage can prevent visualization of the posterior eye during funduscopic examination.

subtypes.name: Rhegmatogenous retinal detachment
subtypes.distinguishing_features: A defect in the neurosensory retina allows vitreous fluid to collect between the sensory and pigmented retinal layers.

subtypes.name: Exudative (serous) retinal detachment
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Subretinal fluid accumulates without a break in the neurosensory epithelium. An underlying inflammatory, infectious, neoplastic, vascular or degenerative process may be responsible.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Establish the diagnosis of retinal detachment.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Used in the initial clinical assessment.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Establish the diagnosis when funduscopic visualization of the posterior eye is obscured.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: May be used, for example, in the presence of vitreous hemorrhage; avoid if globe rupture is known or suspected.

diagnostic_workup.test: MRI orbits without and with IV contrast
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Characterize a suspected mass or another cause of exudative retinal detachment.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Usually Not Appropriate for the initial evaluation of suspected retinal structural abnormality; it may be used selectively after the initial diagnosis.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Provide high-resolution cross-sectional retinal imaging.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Used by ophthalmologists to assess retinal pathology; the guideline does not assign it an appropriateness category for this variant.

long_term_effects: Permanent vision loss can result if an acute retinal detachment is not treated promptly.

conditions.name: Central retinal artery occlusion
conditions.description: A retinal vascular cause of acute visual loss whose initial diagnosis is clinical and funduscopic rather than radiologic.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Sudden painless loss of vision in one eye with an afferent pupillary defect.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Contribute to the initial diagnosis together with clinical presentation.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: At initial evaluation.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Exclude intracranial hemorrhage before IV fibrinolytic therapy.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: May be performed before that treatment, although it is Usually Not Appropriate as initial imaging for the retinal structural abnormality variant.

conditions.name: Optic neuritis (ON)
conditions.description: Inflammation affecting the optic nerve may have demyelinating, antibody-mediated, systemic inflammatory or infectious causes. Enhancement patterns can assist in distinguishing etiologies, although findings overlap.
conditions.clinical_presentation: May cause acute visual loss. The distribution of optic nerve involvement varies by underlying cause.

subtypes.name: MS
subtypes.distinguishing_features: ON associated with MS more characteristically involves a shorter unilateral segment and may affect the anterior optic nerve.

subtypes.name: NMO
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Longer segments and simultaneous bilateral involvement occur more often than with MS; posterior optic nerves, the chiasm or tracts are more characteristic sites.

subtypes.name: MOGAD
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Longer or simultaneous bilateral involvement occurs more often than with MS. Optic nerve sheath or perioptic enhancement is more distinctive, and anterior nerve involvement is more characteristic.

subtypes.name: Chronic relapsing-remitting inflammatory ON
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Listed separately from steroid-dependent, recurrent ON.

diagnostic_workup.test: MRI orbits without and with IV contrast
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Detect optic nerve lesions and enhancement and help differentiate causes of ON.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Usually Appropriate as initial imaging when optic nerve disease is suspected.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Enhancement suggests an acute lesion; the site and pattern of enhancement can help distinguish etiologies. Noncontrast imaging cannot reliably distinguish acute from chronic ON lesions.

diagnostic_workup.test: MRI head without and with IV contrast
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess associated intracranial manifestations and white matter lesions.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: May Be Appropriate concurrently with or after orbital MRI.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Brain MRI features and lesion number can inform the risk of developing MS after a first acute ON episode; an unoptimized routine head examination is less sensitive for ON than dedicated orbital MRI.

diagnostic_workup.test: MRI of the brain and spine
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Detect associated abnormalities when a demyelinating or antibody-mediated etiology is considered.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: May be performed alongside the optic nerve assessment.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess optic nerve disorders.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Has been used to diagnose ON; it is not assigned an appropriateness category in the variant table.

conditions.name: Optic perineuritis
conditions.description: Inflammation around the optic nerve may be associated with idiopathic orbital inflammation, autoimmune disease, infection or another inflammatory cause. Its symptoms can resemble acute demyelinating ON.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Vision loss and pain aggravated by eye movement may occur. Patients tend to be older and are more likely to retain central vision than patients with acute demyelinating ON.

diagnostic_workup.test: MRI orbits without and with IV contrast
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Distinguish perioptic inflammation from disease centered within the optic nerve.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Usually Appropriate as initial imaging for suspected optic nerve abnormality.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Enhancement with indistinct margins along the nerve sheath, sometimes with additional retrobulbar or orbital enhancement, favors optic perineuritis over acute ON centered in the nerve.

conditions.name: Ischemic optic neuropathy
conditions.description: Ischemic injury of the optic nerve is categorized by whether it affects the optic nerve head or the retrobulbar nerve. Both locations may have arteritic or nonarteritic causes.
conditions.clinical_presentation: AION classically produces optic disc edema and an altitudinal visual field defect.

subtypes.name: Anterior ischemic optic neuropathy [AION]
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Ischemia occurs at the optic nerve head. Optic nerve head enhancement can occur in both arteritic and nonarteritic disease but is more consistently observed in the arteritic form.

subtypes.name: Posterior ischemic optic neuropathy [PION]
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Ischemia affects the retrobulbar portion of the optic nerve.

subtypes.name: Nonarteritic
subtypes.distinguishing_features: The document associates this category with underlying vascular risk factors such as hypertension and diabetes.

subtypes.name: Arteritic
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Giant cell arteritis is the most commonly identified cause in this category.

diagnostic_workup.test: MRI orbits without and with IV contrast
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess optic nerve disease and distinguish ischemic neuropathy from other optic nerve disorders.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Usually Appropriate for initial imaging when optic nerve abnormality is suspected.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The enhancement pattern, considered with brain white matter lesions, can help distinguish AION from ON. In a cited study of AION, optic disc restricted diffusion was seen in 71% of patients imaged within 5 days of symptom onset versus approximately 4% of patients imaged later.

diagnostic_workup.test: MRI head without and with IV contrast
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess concurrent brain findings that may help distinguish AION from ON.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: May Be Appropriate as a complementary examination.

diagnostic_workup.test: CTA head and neck with IV contrast; MRA head and neck with IV contrast; MRA head and neck without and with IV contrast; MRA head and neck without IV contrast
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess vascular disease.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Usually Not Appropriate as initial imaging for suspected optic nerve abnormality; vascular assessment may follow in cases of ischemic optic neuropathy.

conditions.name: Optic nerve gliomas
conditions.description: The document identifies these as the most common primary optic nerve neoplasm. In adults, gliomas are more likely to be malignant, making assessment of enhancement important.
conditions.clinical_presentation: They may be detected incidentally, including in younger patients with neurofibromatosis type 1, or present with visual changes or proptosis. Neoplastic visual loss typically develops more slowly than other optic neuropathies.

diagnostic_workup.test: MRI orbits without and with IV contrast
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess the lesion and identify enhancement that may suggest a higher-grade neoplasm.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Usually Appropriate for initial imaging of suspected optic nerve disease.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: An expansile mass inseparable from the optic nerve in a patient with chronic progressive visual loss can favor optic nerve glioma; IV contrast is needed to evaluate enhancement.

conditions.name: Optic nerve sheath meningiomas
conditions.description: Orbital meningiomas may originate from the optic nerve sheath or extend into the orbit from an intracranial mass.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Symptomatic involvement of the optic nerve sheath classically causes painless, progressively worsening vision over a chronic period.

diagnostic_workup.test: MRI orbits without and with IV contrast
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Characterize the lesion and show its extent, including involvement of the orbital apex or intracranial structures.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Usually Appropriate as initial imaging for suspected optic nerve or sheath disease.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Show sheath enhancement and calcification.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Usually Not Appropriate as initial imaging for the suspected optic nerve abnormality variant.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: CT may show characteristic tram track enhancement; nerve sheath calcifications may be present in up to half of cases.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Detect optic nerve sheath calcification.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Usually Not Appropriate as initial imaging for the suspected optic nerve abnormality variant.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Calcification, present in up to half of cases, supports this diagnosis.

conditions.name: Bitemporal hemianopia or junctional scotoma
conditions.description: These visual field abnormalities can result from compression of, or pathology within, the optic chiasm or the junction between the optic nerve and chiasm. The variant addresses suspected sellar or parasellar disease.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Bitemporal hemianopia or junctional scotoma may accompany a sellar or suprasellar mass. Most neoplastic causes develop with gradually progressive visual symptoms; pituitary apoplexy may instead produce headache and rapid visual change.

subtypes.name: Pituitary macroadenomas
subtypes.distinguishing_features: May extend above the sella and compress the optic chiasm or neighboring optic nerves or tracts.

subtypes.name: Sellar/suprasellar region meningiomas
subtypes.distinguishing_features: May involve sellar, suprasellar or parasellar structures and exert mass effect on the optic nerves or chiasm.

subtypes.name: Craniopharyngiomas
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Suprasellar masses that commonly compress the optic chiasm; the papillary type described in adults is usually solid and enhancing and rarely calcifies.

subtypes.name: Pituitary apoplexy
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Often follows hemorrhagic infarction of an existing adenoma and may cause rapid enlargement, headache and visual changes.

subtypes.name: Aneurysms
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Large lesions of the internal carotid artery or Circle of Willis vessels can compress the optic nerves or chiasm.

diagnostic_workup.test: MRI sella without and with IV contrast
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Characterize suspected sellar or parasellar pathology, its extent and its relationship to the optic chiasm and neighboring structures.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Usually Appropriate and the preferred initial imaging examination.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The small-field-of-view, thin-section protocol provides greater anatomical detail than routine head MRI.

diagnostic_workup.test: MRI head without and with IV contrast
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess disease extending beyond the sella, including granulomatous, metastatic or lymphomatous processes.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: May Be Appropriate.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Routine head MRI can identify a large pituitary macroadenoma but generally provides less sellar detail than a dedicated protocol.

diagnostic_workup.test: CTA head with IV contrast; MRA head with IV contrast; MRA head without IV contrast
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Establish whether a lesion suggested by initial MRI is an aneurysm.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: These vascular studies are not recommended by the variant table as routine initial imaging; CTA or MRA may follow MRI if aneurysm is suspected.

diagnostic_workup.test: CT sella without IV contrast; CT sella with IV contrast
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Provide complementary information on calcification, bone invasion or a mass of osseous origin; noncontrast CT may reveal acute hemorrhage in pituitary apoplexy.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Usually Not Appropriate as routine initial imaging for this variant.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: MRI is more sensitive for diagnosing pituitary apoplexy and can assess an underlying pituitary mass.

conditions.name: Homonymous hemianopia
conditions.description: This visual field deficit suggests a retrochiasmatic lesion affecting the optic tracts, lateral geniculate nucleus, optic radiations or primary visual cortex. The document discusses localization and refers comprehensive cerebrovascular imaging guidance to other ACR topics.
conditions.epidemiology: Infarction is identified as the most common cause. Other described causes include hematoma, trauma and brain tumor, with neurosurgical procedures and demyelinating disease mentioned as less common causes.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Visual acuity is usually relatively preserved. An acute onset should raise concern for stroke, although the patient may not immediately recognize the field deficit.

subtypes.name: Occipital lobe hemianopia
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Most commonly attributed to ischemic stroke in the posterior cerebral artery distribution.

diagnostic_workup.test: Imaging of the occipital lobes, optic radiations, optic tracts, or lateral geniculate nucleus
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Locate retrochiasmatic pathology and guide diagnosis and management.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When a homonymous visual field defect is present.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The document does not specify a dedicated initial-imaging variant or modality rating for this presentation.

document_sections.heading: American College of Radiology ACR Appropriateness Criteria® Vision Loss
document_sections.content: The guideline addresses initial imaging for adults with vision loss across 6 clinical variants. Its procedure tables assign an Appropriateness Category and Relative Radiation Level to each examination.

document_sections.heading: Variant 1: Adult. Acute posttraumatic visual defect. Suspect orbital injury. Initial imaging.
document_sections.content: For initial assessment, CT maxillofacial without IV contrast and CT orbits without IV contrast are Usually Appropriate alternatives. CT head without IV contrast is May Be Appropriate. The table rates facial and orbital radiography, cerebral arteriography, the listed MRA and MRI examinations, contrast-enhanced or multiphase CT examinations, and the listed CTA examinations Usually Not Appropriate. It also reports each examination's Relative Radiation Level.

document_sections.heading: Variant 2: Adult. Acute vision loss. Infection or inflammatory disorder suspected. Initial imaging.
document_sections.content: MRI orbits without and with IV contrast, CT maxillofacial with IV contrast, and CT orbits with IV contrast are Usually Appropriate. MRI head without and with IV contrast and CT orbits without IV contrast are May Be Appropriate. All remaining examinations in this variant's table are Usually Not Appropriate. The table also assigns a Relative Radiation Level to every listed examination.

document_sections.heading: Variant 3: Adult. Chronic or progressive unilateral vision loss. Intraorbital mass-like lesion suspected or vascular lesion suspected. Initial imaging.
document_sections.content: MRI orbits without and with IV contrast is Usually Appropriate. MRI head without and with IV contrast and CT orbits with IV contrast are May Be Appropriate. Every other procedure in the table is Usually Not Appropriate; the table also gives their Relative Radiation Levels.

document_sections.heading: Variant 4: Adult. Acute vision loss, retinal structural abnormality suspected. Initial imaging.
document_sections.content: Every cross-sectional imaging examination listed for this presentation is Usually Not Appropriate for initial imaging. The table supplies the Relative Radiation Level of each examination.

document_sections.heading: Variant 5: Adult. Acute or chronic vision loss, optic nerve abnormality suspected. Initial imaging.
document_sections.content: MRI orbits without and with IV contrast is Usually Appropriate, while MRI head without and with IV contrast is May Be Appropriate. Every other listed examination is Usually Not Appropriate. Relative Radiation Levels accompany the procedure ratings.

document_sections.heading: Variant 6: Adult. Bitemporal hemianopia or junctional scotoma. Sellar or parasellar mass suspected. Initial imaging.
document_sections.content: MRI sella without and with IV contrast is Usually Appropriate. MRI head without and with IV contrast is May Be Appropriate. The remaining procedures in the table are Usually Not Appropriate; their Relative Radiation Levels are also provided.

document_sections.heading: Summary of Literature Review Introduction/Background
document_sections.content: Vision loss has many possible causes. A meta-analysis of 2017 data estimated that more than 7 million people in the United States had vision loss, defined as visual acuity ≤20/40 in the better-seeing eye. Whether imaging is needed, and which examination to choose, depends on symptom acuity, clinical presentation, suspected cause, and the likely site of injury along the visual pathway. Characteristic visual-field patterns aid localization and guide imaging and differential diagnosis. Most nontraumatic globe disorders are assessed ophthalmologically without cross-sectional imaging unless complications are suspected. CT best evaluates bone, calcification, and radio-opaque foreign bodies; MRI better resolves soft tissues. CTA, MRA, and DSA can investigate vascular causes, with DSA serving as the reference standard. This guideline concentrates on presentations in which vision loss is the principal symptom; separate ACR topics address headache and associated intracranial hypertension or papilledema, head trauma, and other overlapping conditions. Homonymous hemianopia suggests a retrochiasmatic abnormality of the optic tracts, lateral geniculate nucleus, optic radiations, or occipital primary visual cortex, usually with relatively preserved acuity. Infarction is its most frequent cause; other causes include hematoma, trauma, tumor, and, less commonly, neurosurgical procedures or demyelination. Occipital hemianopia most often follows ischemia in the posterior cerebral artery territory, whereas infarction in the middle cerebral artery territory most often affects the optic radiations. Dural sinus or cerebral vein thrombosis can cause frequently hemorrhagic venous infarction; thrombosis in the posterior superior sagittal sinus can affect the occipital cortex. Sudden symptoms raise concern for stroke, although a patient may not immediately notice hemianopia. Imaging can detect retrochiasmatic pathology responsible for complete or incomplete homonymous hemianopia and inform treatment. Other ACR topics cover the full imaging approach to transient ischemic attack, stroke, acute cerebrovascular disease, and brain tumors.

document_sections.heading: Special Imaging Considerations
document_sections.content: The clinician may select CT maxillofacial or CT orbits. Institutional protocols determine reconstruction thickness and field of view: maxillofacial CT typically covers from above the frontal sinuses through the mandible, whereas orbital CT generally has a smaller, orbit-centered field and may omit some facial bones. Orbital MRI protocols vary, but commonly combine axial and coronal T1-weighted images without fat suppression, fat-suppressed coronal T2-weighted images for optic nerve assessment, axial T2-weighted images with or without fat suppression, and DWI within a small orbital field. Postcontrast orbital images should suppress fat so that enhancement remains visible. Ocular US is outside the variant tables and this guideline's scope; ophthalmologists, and sometimes clinicians trained in advanced emergency US, perform it. It can identify lens dislocation, vitreous hemorrhage, retinal detachment, foreign bodies, retrobulbar hematoma, and papilledema. It assesses orbital-floor fractures much less completely than CT. It can also evaluate optic nerve or extraocular-muscle disorders and orbital masses, while color Doppler adds assessment of ocular and retinal vascular abnormalities. Avoid ocular US when globe rupture is known or suspected. Ophthalmologists use near-infrared light in optical coherence tomography to produce high-resolution retinal cross-sections; beyond retinal disease, it has been used to diagnose optic nerve disorders such as ON.

document_sections.heading: Initial Imaging Definition
document_sections.content: Initial imaging occurs at the start of care for the condition specified by a variant. More than one examination may be Usually Appropriate when the examinations are equivalent alternatives, of which only one is ordered, or complementary examinations obtained together because each contributes different information.

document_sections.heading: Discussion of Procedures by Variant
document_sections.content: The following sections explain the clinical circumstances, evidence, and limitations underlying the initial-imaging ratings for each variant.

document_sections.heading: Variant 1: Adult. Acute posttraumatic visual defect. Suspect orbital injury. Initial imaging.
document_sections.content: Orbital fractures most often follow assault or a direct blow, motor-vehicle collisions, falls, or sports injuries. They can occur alone or alongside zygomaticomaxillary complex, Le Fort II and III, or nasoethmoidal complex fractures. Diplopia can accompany depressed orbital-floor fractures, especially anterior- or middle-third injuries and small- to medium-sized defects with soft-tissue herniation. Fractures >2 cm are more likely to produce enophthalmos. Blowout injury can involve the lamina papyracea, but extraocular-muscle herniation and serious immediate complications are less common than with orbital-floor blowout fractures. Most orbital fractures can undergo delayed repair after swelling improves; CT can reveal injuries needing more urgent action, including trapdoor fractures and orbital compartment syndrome. Lateral- and superior-wall fractures carry increased traumatic optic neuropathy risk because blunt force can reach the optic canal and shear the nerve. With associated brain injury or obtundation, an afferent pupillary defect may be its sole clinical sign. Urgent diagnosis permits timely intervention when needed. Although optic-canal fractures increase nerve-injury risk, emergency surgery for traumatic optic neuropathy is generally reserved for a bone fragment impinging on the nerve, hematoma in the canal, or enlarging retrobulbar hematoma with proptosis. Severe proptosis with posterior globe tenting requires emergency orbital decompression to preserve vision. An orbital-apex fracture involving the superior orbital fissure can affect multiple traversing cranial nerves. Retrobulbar hematoma, emphysema, or a blow-in fracture can increase orbital mass effect and cause compartment syndrome and vision loss. Imaging evidence of retrobulbar bleeding does not sensitively predict subsequent compartment syndrome: diagnose it from clinical evidence of optic nerve compression. Extraocular-muscle entrapment after an orbital-floor fracture is likewise a clinical diagnosis; muscle herniation and altered contour have low positive predictive values for entrapment. Imaging aims to identify orbital injuries and complications early enough to guide timely care and prevent permanent visual loss.

document_sections.heading: Arteriography Cerebral
document_sections.content: For initial imaging of posttraumatic vision loss, relevant literature does not support cerebral arteriography. DSA can diagnose a traumatic vascular lesion such as a carotid cavernous fistula, but is not a first-line examination.

document_sections.heading: CT Head With IV Contrast
document_sections.content: Relevant literature does not support this examination as initial imaging for posttraumatic vision loss.

document_sections.heading: CT Head Without and With IV Contrast
document_sections.content: Relevant literature does not support this examination as initial imaging for posttraumatic vision loss.

document_sections.heading: CT Head Without IV Contrast
document_sections.content: The injury mechanism may put patients with orbital or facial fractures at increased risk of brain injury, intracranial hemorrhage, and skull fracture. In a single-emergency-department study of more than 1,600 consecutive patients with traumatic brain injury, CT detected at least 1 facial fracture in 200 patients (12.1%). Of those 200 patients, 166 (83%) needed dedicated maxillofacial CT for diagnosis; of those 166 patients, 73 (44%) required surgery. Patients with facial fractures more often had initial loss of consciousness, abnormal head CT or physical examination, and a lower Glasgow Coma Scale score. In another study of 1,220 patients with orbital-wall fractures and no known traumatic brain injury, associated intracranial injury was present in 62 of 677 patients who underwent head CT (9%); orbital-roof fracture, frontal-bone fracture, and older age independently increased that risk. Routine orbital or maxillofacial CT generally omits parts of the head and brain, whereas head CT may omit parts of the orbits and usually does not cover the entire lower face. With facial trauma and known or suspected traumatic brain injury, concurrent noncontrast head and maxillofacial CT are usually indicated.

document_sections.heading: CT Maxillofacial With IV Contrast
document_sections.content: Relevant literature does not support its use for initial imaging of posttraumatic vision loss.

document_sections.heading: CT Maxillofacial Without and With IV Contrast
document_sections.content: Relevant literature does not support its use for initial imaging of posttraumatic vision loss.

document_sections.heading: CT Maxillofacial Without IV Contrast
document_sections.content: MDCT rapidly detects acute orbital fractures and soft-tissue injury and permits multiplanar reconstructions from one head position and acquisition plane; other body regions can also be imaged during polytrauma assessment. Blunt-trauma orbital fractures frequently coexist with midfacial and possibly mandibular fractures that an orbital CT field might not fully cover. Depending on the mechanism, noncontrast maxillofacial or orbital CT can be useful initially, provided the field includes the full extent of suspected injury. CT localizes radio-opaque intraorbital foreign bodies and displaced bone fragments. It can also reveal intraocular hemorrhage or detachment, lens displacement, open-globe injury, retrobulbar or subperiosteal hematoma, extraocular-muscle injury or herniation, and findings concerning for optic nerve injury.

document_sections.heading: CT Orbits With IV Contrast
document_sections.content: Relevant literature does not support its use for initial imaging of posttraumatic vision loss.

document_sections.heading: CT Orbits Without and With IV Contrast
document_sections.content: Relevant literature does not support its use for initial imaging of posttraumatic vision loss.

document_sections.heading: CT Orbits Without IV Contrast
document_sections.content: MDCT quickly evaluates fractures and soft tissues after acute orbital trauma and enables multiplanar reconstructions; additional regions can be scanned in polytrauma. Associated midfacial or mandibular fractures may fall outside the orbital field. Orbit-limited CT may suffice after a direct orbital impact without concern for other facial fractures, or after penetrating orbital injury. If additional facial injury is clinically suspected, the wider maxillofacial study is more useful. CT can locate radio-opaque foreign bodies and bone fragments and show traumatic globe injury, hemorrhage, detachment, lens dislocation, open-globe injury, retrobulbar or subperiosteal hematoma, extraocular-muscle injury or herniation, and possible optic nerve injury.

document_sections.heading: CTA Head With IV Contrast
document_sections.content: Relevant literature does not support initial CTA head for posttraumatic vision loss. It may nevertheless help diagnose a posttraumatic vascular lesion such as a carotid cavernous fistula, or investigate suspected vascular injury when a fracture reaches the skull base.

document_sections.heading: MRI Head Without IV Contrast
document_sections.content: Relevant literature does not support initial use for posttraumatic vision loss. After initial head CT, it may be warranted to examine associated intracranial injuries, including subtle traumatic abnormalities less apparent on noncontrast CT. Routine head MRI protocols differ between institutions; their coronal T2 images, when included, typically have thicker sections than orbital MRI and lack fat suppression, making them less suitable for evaluating optic nerve T2 abnormalities.

document_sections.heading: MRI Orbits Without IV Contrast
document_sections.content: Orbital MRI can assess visual pathways and suspected traumatic optic neuropathy. Following penetrating injury, exclude a metallic foreign body before performing it. High-resolution coronal T2-weighted orbital imaging, preferably with fat suppression, can show abnormal optic nerve signal. In the appropriate clinical setting, optic nerve diffusion restriction is highly specific but insensitive for traumatic optic neuropathy. CT better depicts associated fracture or bone fragments, whereas MRI is more sensitive than CT for nonradiopaque foreign bodies, choroidal or retinal detachment, and open-globe injury. Initial imaging is noncontrast maxillofacial or orbital CT; orbital MRI is generally a secondary study for traumatic optic neuropathy.

document_sections.heading: Radiography Face
document_sections.content: Relevant literature does not support facial radiography initially after traumatic vision loss. It detects orbital and facial fractures less sensitively than CT and does not assess soft tissues. It can show a radio-opaque orbital foreign body but cannot localize that object against surrounding soft tissue as CT can.

document_sections.heading: Radiography Orbit
document_sections.content: Relevant literature does not support orbital radiography initially after traumatic vision loss. Relative to CT, it is less sensitive for orbital fractures, cannot evaluate soft tissues, and cannot precisely localize a visible radio-opaque foreign body relative to soft tissues.

document_sections.heading: Variant 2: Adult. Acute vision loss. Infection or inflammatory disorder suspected. Initial imaging.
document_sections.content: Orbital infection can cause cellulitis, subperiosteal abscess, or orbital abscess and is an ophthalmologic emergency because of potential visual loss and intracranial complications, including meningitis, cerebritis, intracranial abscess, and cavernous sinus thrombosis. Pain and swelling near the orbit, reduced acuity, and ophthalmoplegia may occur. Infection most commonly spreads from adjacent structures, often from bacterial paranasal sinus disease. Clinical and imaging differentiation of periorbital from postseptal disease helps determine whether inpatient IV antibiotics are needed. Subperiosteal abscess usually needs surgical drainage. Acute invasive fungal sinusitis can also cause orbital complications; it is aggressive, associated with high mortality, and typically affects immunocompromised patients. Orbital inflammation can be idiopathic or secondary to granulomatous, inflammatory, or autoimmune disease, including sarcoidosis, IgG4-related disease, or Graves’ disease. Its manifestations and risk of visual loss depend on the cause and affected orbital structures. Cellulitis, orbital inflammatory syndrome, and lymphoproliferative lesions may overlap clinically and radiologically. Imaging seeks to define disease extent and complications, particularly abscess, to guide intervention and avert lasting vision loss, intracranial extension, or cavernous sinus thrombosis.

document_sections.heading: CT Head With IV Contrast
document_sections.content: Relevant literature does not support its initial use for infectious or inflammatory vision loss. Head CT may not encompass the whole orbit and is not preferred for orbital assessment; MRI is preferred when investigating intracranial spread.

document_sections.heading: CT Maxillofacial With IV Contrast
document_sections.content: In the emergency setting, contrast-enhanced CT is a first-line examination for acute vision loss associated with orbital infection or inflammation. Its spatial resolution helps distinguish periorbital from postseptal infection, informing inpatient versus outpatient antibiotic care. It shows neighboring sinus disease and bone erosion; IV contrast helps detect abscesses needing urgent surgery and enlargement with absent enhancement of a thrombosed superior ophthalmic vein. MRI better depicts orbital inflammatory extent, intracranial spread, and small abscesses. Orbital CT ordinarily covers enough anatomy, but maxillofacial CT is warranted when the suspected source or disease extent lies outside the orbital field, which may omit the lower maxillary sinus and maxillary teeth.

document_sections.heading: CT Maxillofacial Without IV Contrast
document_sections.content: Relevant literature does not support initial noncontrast maxillofacial CT for this presentation; IV contrast is preferred. Without contrast, CT may still depict inflamed soft tissues, neighboring sinus disease, and bone erosion, but has less ability to distinguish an abscess from other inflammatory change.

document_sections.heading: CT Orbits With IV Contrast
document_sections.content: Contrast-enhanced orbital CT is a first-line emergency examination for vision loss from suspected orbital infection or inflammation. It distinguishes periorbital from postseptal involvement to inform antibiotic setting, and identifies adjacent sinus disease, osseous erosion, abscesses that may need urgent surgery, and possible superior ophthalmic vein thrombosis manifested by enlargement and lack of enhancement. MRI provides better soft-tissue contrast, assessment of intracranial extension, and visualization of small abscesses. If the suspected source or inflammation extends beyond the orbital CT field, including into the lower maxillary sinus or maxillary dentition, maxillofacial CT is warranted.

document_sections.heading: CT Orbits Without IV Contrast
document_sections.content: IV contrast is preferred for suspected orbital infection or inflammation. Noncontrast CT can nevertheless show inflammatory soft-tissue changes, adjacent sinus disease, and osseous erosion, though it is less capable of separating abscess from other inflammation. For suspected thyroid orbitopathy, noncontrast orbital CT sufficiently shows many characteristic findings, including enlarged extraocular muscles, prolapsed lacrimal gland, increased orbital fat, and proptosis.

document_sections.heading: CTA Head With IV Contrast
document_sections.content: Relevant literature does not support initial CTA head in infectious or inflammatory vision loss. If clinical or initial imaging findings raise concern for arterial complications, it can assess internal carotid artery narrowing or occlusion. Depending on acquisition timing, CTA may also diagnose venous abnormalities such as superior ophthalmic vein thrombosis.

document_sections.heading: CTV Head With IV Contrast
document_sections.content: Relevant literature does not support its initial use for this presentation. When clinical findings and initial imaging suggest venous complications of orbital cellulitis or inflammation, CTV head can investigate superior ophthalmic vein or cavernous sinus thrombosis.

document_sections.heading: MRA Head With IV Contrast
document_sections.content: Relevant literature does not support initial use. MRA head can be performed if intracranial spread raises concern for arterial complications, such as internal carotid artery abnormalities near the cavernous sinus; that concern usually follows initial orbital and/or head MRI. Noncontrast TOF MRA has better spatial resolution than contrast-enhanced MRA. In a retrospective study of 123 patients, TOF and contrast-enhanced MRA had similar sensitivity for intracranial arterial occlusion. In that study, contrast-enhanced MRA agreed more closely with DSA on distal internal carotid artery occlusion location, while performance at other intracranial occlusion sites was similar.

document_sections.heading: MRA Head Without and With IV Contrast
document_sections.content: Relevant literature does not support initial use for infectious or inflammatory vision loss. MRA head may assess suspected arterial complications of intracranial spread, including internal carotid artery abnormalities associated with cavernous sinus involvement. Acquiring both noncontrast and contrast-enhanced head MRA is unnecessary.

document_sections.heading: MRA Head Without IV Contrast
document_sections.content: Relevant literature does not support its initial use. After initial orbital and/or head MRI, noncontrast head MRA may assess suspected arterial complications from intracranial extension, including internal carotid artery abnormalities. Noncontrast TOF MRA offers higher spatial resolution than contrast-enhanced MRA. In a retrospective study of 123 patients, the techniques had similar sensitivity for intracranial arterial occlusion; contrast-enhanced MRA correlated more closely with DSA for the location of distal internal carotid artery occlusion, but other occlusion sites showed similar performance.

document_sections.heading: MRI Head Without and With IV Contrast
document_sections.content: Head MRI without and with IV contrast can investigate suspected intracranial extension or complications concurrently with, or after, orbital MRI. Postcontrast images show meningeal disease, more clearly define infection or inflammation, improve assessment of cavernous sinus thrombosis, and supplement DWI when separating abscess from phlegmon. Contrast-enhanced head MRI with a 3-D T1 gradient echo sequence has shown high sensitivity and specificity for dural venous sinus thrombosis. For cavernous sinus thrombosis, head MRI without and with IV contrast is the preferred cross-sectional test; findings include sinus engorgement, convexity of its lateral wall, and postcontrast filling defects.

document_sections.heading: MRI Head Without IV Contrast
document_sections.content: Relevant literature does not support initial noncontrast head MRI for infectious or inflammatory vision loss. For intracranial spread, MRI without and with IV contrast is preferred because postcontrast images reveal meningeal involvement, better define disease, improve cavernous sinus thrombosis diagnosis, and complement DWI in distinguishing abscess from phlegmon.

document_sections.heading: MRI Orbits Without and With IV Contrast
document_sections.content: Orbital MRI optimally evaluates the extent and complications of infection or inflammation when obtained before and after IV contrast. Its orbital field, sections, and sequences suit intraorbital disease better than MRI of the neck, face, or a routine head protocol. It provides the strongest soft-tissue contrast and useful anatomic resolution; thinner sections and fat-suppressed T2-weighted and postcontrast T1-weighted sequences favor orbital over routine head MRI. DWI and postcontrast images help distinguish abscess from edema or phlegmon; DWI with apparent diffusion coefficient values may help separate orbital inflammatory syndrome, cellulitis, and lymphoproliferative disease. Orbital MRI with IV contrast can show superior ophthalmic vein enlargement and absent enhancement from thrombosis. Add head imaging when intracranial complications warrant evaluation.

document_sections.heading: MRI Orbits Without IV Contrast
document_sections.content: MRI is preferred for defining orbital inflammation, disease extent, and complications, and orbital protocols outperform routine head MRI for this purpose through thinner sections, higher resolution, and fat-saturated T2 imaging. Noncontrast sequences provide some information, including DWI, but imaging should include both precontrast and postcontrast acquisitions. DWI together with postcontrast imaging better separates abscess from edema and phlegmon; noncontrast orbital MRI is less optimal. Head imaging may be added when intracranial complications are suspected.

document_sections.heading: MRV Head With IV Contrast
document_sections.content: Relevant literature does not support initial use. Follow-up MRV head may help when an intracranial venous complication such as cavernous sinus thrombosis is suspected. Among MRI sequences, contrast-enhanced MRV using a 3-D T1 gradient echo sequence has shown the highest combination of sensitivity and specificity for dural venous sinus thrombosis. If the institution's postcontrast head MRI already includes that sequence, dedicated MRV is unlikely to add substantial diagnostic information for cavernous or dural sinus thrombosis.

document_sections.heading: MRV Head Without and With IV Contrast
document_sections.content: Relevant literature does not support its initial use. Noncontrast MRV has limited ability to detect cavernous sinus thrombosis; contrast-enhanced MRI/MRV can show heterogeneous filling defects.

document_sections.heading: MRV Head Without IV Contrast
document_sections.content: Relevant literature does not support its initial use. This noncontrast study is limited for cavernous sinus thrombosis detection, whereas contrast-enhanced MRI/MRV can demonstrate heterogeneous filling defects.

document_sections.heading: Variant 3: Adult. Chronic or progressive unilateral vision loss. Intraorbital mass-like lesion suspected or vascular lesion suspected. Initial imaging.
document_sections.content: Many tumors, tumor-like conditions, systemic diseases, metastases, and high- or low-flow vascular malformations can involve the orbit. Distinguishing vascular from other lesions guides subsequent workup and care. Because the orbital space is restricted, either a soft-tissue or vascular mass may cause proptosis. Orbital-apex masses or inflammation characteristically produce vision loss with ophthalmoplegia. Orbital masses can be classified by location in the globe, optic nerve sheath complex, intraconal or extraconal space, bone, or multiple compartments. Benign lesions predominate, but malignant orbital tumors become more prevalent in adults older than 60 years of age. Among cysts, dermoid cysts are most common; excluding cysts, cavernous venous malformation is the commonest benign adult orbital mass, while non-Hodgkin lymphoma is the commonest malignant one. Imaging seeks to detect and characterize the causative orbital mass or vascular lesion, direct care, and sometimes establish a specific diagnosis.

document_sections.heading: CT Maxillofacial With IV Contrast
document_sections.content: Relevant literature does not support its initial use for chronic or progressive unilateral vision loss. Orbit-centered masses generally need the section thickness and field of view supplied by orbital CT; a large facial mass extending into the orbit calls for wider maxillofacial coverage.

document_sections.heading: CT Orbits With IV Contrast
document_sections.content: Orbital MRI without and with IV contrast is generally first-line for suspected mass or vascular lesion because it better resolves soft tissues and distinguishes orbital compartments. CT can contribute complementary information and is preferred for orbital calcification or osseous masses. CT obtained without and during a Valsalva maneuver can diagnose orbital venous varix, while dynamic postcontrast CT can show the progressive enhancement characteristic of cavernous venous malformation. Rapidly progressive vision loss may also justify CT as first-line imaging.

document_sections.heading: CT Orbits Without and With IV Contrast
document_sections.content: Relevant literature does not support this combined CT protocol initially. If orbital CT is used for a mass, an IV contrast-enhanced examination is sufficient. Orbital MRI without and with IV contrast is generally first-line because of superior soft-tissue resolution.

document_sections.heading: CT Orbits Without IV Contrast
document_sections.content: Relevant literature does not support initial noncontrast orbital CT. Contrast-enhanced orbital MRI is first-line for suspected mass or vascular lesion; CT is particularly useful for calcifications and is preferred for masses originating in bone. If orbital CT is obtained, it should use IV contrast.

document_sections.heading: CTA Head With IV Contrast
document_sections.content: Relevant literature does not support initial CTA head for chronic or progressive unilateral vision loss. It may have a role in secondary assessment of a high-flow orbital vascular lesion such as an arteriovenous malformation.

document_sections.heading: FDG-PET/CT Skull to Mid-Thigh
document_sections.content: Relevant literature does not support initial FDG-PET/CT. For primary orbital masses, it offers no significant diagnostic advantage over clinical evaluation combined with CT/MRI, and its spatial resolution is limited for the small orbital compartment. It may detect metastases missed by other modalities and contributes to orbital lymphoma staging. FDG uptake does not specifically indicate malignancy: benign masses and infectious or inflammatory conditions may also be avid. Other pitfalls include overlapping uptake in malignancy and inflammation, low uptake by small lesions, interference from avid extraocular muscles, and incomplete evaluation near the edge of the field in standard skull-to-upper-thigh scans.

document_sections.heading: MRI Head Without and With IV Contrast
document_sections.content: Head MRI can assess intracranial extension of an orbital mass. If ordered for that purpose, it should include acquisitions without and with IV contrast to provide the most information.

document_sections.heading: MRI Head Without IV Contrast
document_sections.content: Relevant literature does not support initial noncontrast head MRI for this presentation. When assessing intracranial spread of an orbital mass, obtain head MRI without and with IV contrast.

document_sections.heading: MRI Orbits Without and With IV Contrast
document_sections.content: For chronic or progressive unilateral loss of vision with a suspected orbital mass or vascular lesion, orbital MRI before and after IV contrast is the initial test of choice. Compared with CT, it better resolves soft tissues and determines lesion extent. Its thin sections, higher resolution, fat-saturated T2-weighted images, and postcontrast T1-weighted images also favor it over routine head MRI. Comprehensive assessment requires both noncontrast and contrast-enhanced sequences.

document_sections.heading: MRI Orbits Without IV Contrast
document_sections.content: Relevant literature does not support noncontrast orbital MRI alone as initial imaging. Although orbital MRI resolves soft tissues and lesion extent better than CT and has thinner, higher-resolution, fat-saturated T2-weighted images than routine head MRI, complete evaluation of a suspected mass or vascular lesion requires acquisitions without and with IV contrast.

document_sections.heading: Variant 4: Adult. Acute vision loss, retinal structural abnormality suspected. Initial imaging.
document_sections.content: Acute vision loss from retinal detachment is an emergency because delayed treatment can result in permanent impairment. Rhegmatogenous detachment is the most common type: a neurosensory retinal break lets vitreous fluid enter the potential space between sensory and pigmented retina. Clinical assessment and dilated funduscopy establish the diagnosis, ordinarily without imaging.
