If vitreous hemorrhage or another obstacle obscures the posterior eye, ocular US may establish detachment. Exudative or serous detachment instead involves subretinal fluid without a neurosensory epithelial break. Inflammatory, infectious, neoplastic, vascular, or degenerative conditions can disrupt the blood-retinal barrier and cause it. Central retinal artery occlusion presents with abrupt, painless monocular vision loss and an afferent pupillary defect; clinical findings and funduscopy, rather than initial radiologic imaging, establish the diagnosis. IV fibrinolytic therapy may be given within the designated treatment window. For exudative detachment, imaging may identify an underlying choroidal mass or uveomeningeal syndrome after clinical diagnosis. Acute detachment often needs prompt treatment to prevent permanent vision loss.

document_sections.heading: CT Head Without IV Contrast
document_sections.content: Relevant literature does not support its use to initially diagnose a suspected retinal structural abnormality. In acute central retinal artery occlusion, it may be obtained before IV fibrinolytic therapy to exclude intracranial hemorrhage.

document_sections.heading: MRI Orbits Without and With IV Contrast
document_sections.content: Relevant literature does not support its use in the initial diagnostic assessment of a suspected retinal structural abnormality. After that assessment, it may be selected to investigate a mass or other underlying cause of exudative retinal detachment.

document_sections.heading: Variant 5: Adult. Acute or chronic vision loss, optic nerve abnormality suspected. Initial imaging.
document_sections.content: Neoplastic, inflammatory, ischemic, demyelinating, and traumatic processes can affect the optic nerve or its sheath and produce acute, subacute, or chronic visual loss. Neoplasms tend to develop more slowly than other optic neuropathies. Optic nerve gliomas are the most common primary optic nerve neoplasm; they can be incidental, including in younger patients with neurofibromatosis type 1, or present with visual symptoms or proptosis, and are more likely to be malignant when presenting in adults. Orbital meningiomas can arise from the optic nerve sheath or extend from an intracranial mass; symptomatic sheath lesions classically cause gradual, painless visual decline. Inflammatory and demyelinating ON can resemble one another clinically and radiologically; enhancement reflects edema, inflammation, or demyelination. Possible causes of demyelinating ON include MS, NMO, and MOGAD. ON can also reflect chronic relapsing-remitting inflammatory disease, steroid-dependent recurrence, systemic inflammation, or infection. Enhancement patterns overlap but may help: bilateral simultaneous and longer optic nerve involvement occur more often with MOGAD or NMO than MS, which characteristically affects a shorter unilateral segment. Sheath or perioptic enhancement is more distinctive of MOGAD. Anterior involvement is more typical of MS or MOGAD; NMO tends toward posterior nerves, chiasm, or tracts. Brain and spine MRI may identify associated abnormalities; asymptomatic optic nerve lesions may help distinguish relapsing-remitting MS or clinically isolated syndrome from NMO or MOGAD. Optic perineuritis can arise from idiopathic orbital inflammation, autoimmunity, infection, or other inflammation and may mimic acute demyelinating ON, including visual loss and pain worsened by eye movement. Patients with perineuritis tend to be older and more likely to retain central vision. Ischemic optic neuropathy is anterior, AION, when involving the nerve head, or posterior, PION, when involving the retrobulbar nerve. AION classically causes disc edema and altitudinal field loss. Either form may be nonarteritic, in patients with vascular risk factors such as hypertension or diabetes, or arteritic, most commonly from giant cell arteritis. Imaging aims to identify optic nerve disease, narrow overlapping diagnoses, and inform management.

document_sections.heading: CT Orbits With IV Contrast
document_sections.content: Relevant literature does not support its initial use for suspected optic nerve disease. Postcontrast CT may show tram-track enhancement in optic nerve sheath meningioma and sheath calcification, present in up to half of cases; MRI remains first-line because it better resolves soft tissues.

document_sections.heading: CT Orbits Without IV Contrast
document_sections.content: Relevant literature does not support its initial use. CT can demonstrate optic nerve sheath calcification in up to half of optic nerve sheath meningiomas, favoring that diagnosis, but MRI is first-line for suspected nerve or sheath disease because of better soft-tissue resolution.

document_sections.heading: CTA Head and Neck With IV Contrast
document_sections.content: Relevant literature does not support initial use for suspected optic nerve abnormality. After ischemic optic neuropathy is identified, vascular imaging of the head and neck may be performed to assess vascular disease.

document_sections.heading: CTA Head With IV Contrast
document_sections.content: Relevant literature does not support initial use. Subsequent vascular assessment may be performed for ischemic optic neuropathy, but a complete assessment also includes the neck.

document_sections.heading: MRA Head and Neck With IV Contrast
document_sections.content: Relevant literature does not support initial use. Subsequent head and neck vascular imaging may assess vascular disease in ischemic optic neuropathy.

document_sections.heading: MRA Head and Neck Without and With IV Contrast
document_sections.content: Relevant literature does not support initial use. Subsequent head and neck vascular imaging may assess vascular disease in ischemic optic neuropathy.

document_sections.heading: MRA Head and Neck Without IV Contrast
document_sections.content: Relevant literature does not support initial use. Subsequent head and neck vascular imaging may assess vascular disease in ischemic optic neuropathy.

document_sections.heading: MRA Head With IV Contrast
document_sections.content: Relevant literature does not support initial use. Later vascular imaging may investigate ischemic optic neuropathy; comprehensive vascular assessment covers both head and neck.

document_sections.heading: MRA Head Without and With IV Contrast
document_sections.content: Relevant literature does not support initial use. Later vascular imaging may investigate ischemic optic neuropathy; comprehensive vascular assessment covers both head and neck.

document_sections.heading: MRA Head Without IV Contrast
document_sections.content: Relevant literature does not support initial use. Later vascular imaging may investigate ischemic optic neuropathy; comprehensive vascular assessment covers both head and neck.

document_sections.heading: MRI Head Without and With IV Contrast
document_sections.content: Head MRI may accompany or follow orbital MRI, which is the best initial examination for a suspected optic nerve abnormality. For suspected inflammatory or demyelinating ON, head MRI can assess intracranial disease. Brain MRI lesion features and number can predict subsequent MS risk after a first acute ON episode. Postcontrast 3-D Cube T1-weighted whole-brain MRI has shown high sensitivity and accuracy for enhancement in acute ON. Nevertheless, an unoptimized routine head MRI alone detects ON less sensitively than dedicated orbital MRI, with sensitivity dependent on institutional protocol. Combining optic nerve enhancement pattern with cerebral white-matter lesion distribution has shown high accuracy in distinguishing AION from ON.

document_sections.heading: MRI Head Without IV Contrast
document_sections.content: Relevant literature does not support initial noncontrast head MRI for suspected optic nerve abnormality; orbital MRI without and with IV contrast is recommended. Some advocate noncontrast head MRI for follow-up of established demyelinating disease or prior ON to avoid repeated IV gadolinium, but it cannot depict enhancing lesions of acute disease. Standard MS head MRI is less sensitive than coronal STIR for detecting T2-hyperintense optic nerve lesions, especially within the orbit. Routine brain MRI sensitivity also depends on sequences, slice thickness, and other institutional technical factors.

document_sections.heading: MRI Orbits Without and With IV Contrast
document_sections.content: Orbital MRI before and after IV contrast is the imaging test of choice for distinguishing causes of optic nerve-related visual loss. Optic pathway glioma and optic nerve sheath meningioma have characteristic appearances. Because adult optic gliomas may be malignant, IV contrast is important for identifying enhancement suggestive of higher-grade neoplasm; postcontrast imaging best demonstrates meningioma extent into the orbital apex or intracranial space. Dedicated orbital MRI detects T2-hyperintense optic pathway lesions more sensitively than routine head MRI through thinner sections, greater resolution, and fat-saturated T2-weighted and postcontrast T1-weighted sequences. Coronal 2-D STIR is commonly used; 3-D double inversion recovery and 3-D STIR have shown high sensitivity for optic nerve lesions. Contrast-enhanced fluid-attenuated inversion recovery can detect even trace subarachnoid gadolinium and may disclose perioptic enhancement as the sole imaging abnormality. A 3T MRI has shown greater sensitivity for ON lesions than 1.5T MRI. Enhancement suggests acute ON, and its pattern can help distinguish causes before laboratory or antibody results are available. In acute ON, enhancement is centered in the nerve; in optic perineuritis, it has indistinct margins along the sheath and can extend elsewhere in the retrobulbar region or orbit. Optic nerve-head enhancement has been reported more consistently than diffusion restriction in AION, especially arteritic AION. Delayed scanning or omission of dedicated orbital DWI may contribute to unexpectedly low reported diffusion-restriction rates. In a study of AION, optic-disc diffusion restriction occurred in 71% of patients imaged within 5 days after symptom onset versus approximately 4% of those imaged later. Nerve-head enhancement occurs in both arteritic and nonarteritic AION but is more consistently observed in arteritic disease. Combined optic nerve enhancement patterns and brain white-matter lesion distribution have shown high accuracy for separating AION from ON.

document_sections.heading: MRI Orbits Without IV Contrast
document_sections.content: Relevant literature does not support noncontrast orbital MRI alone as the initial test. Although its sequences provide information, postcontrast imaging is necessary for the most complete initial optic nerve assessment. Orbital MRI has thinner, higher-resolution, fat-saturated T2-weighted imaging than routine head MRI. An expansile nerve-associated mass with chronic progressive loss may strongly suggest glioma, but adult gliomas may be malignant and enhancement can suggest higher grade. Nerve or sheath enhancement helps distinguish optic neuropathy and demyelinating ON from optic perineuritis. Noncontrast MRI can detect ON lesions but cannot reliably distinguish acute from chronic disease; enhancement suggests acute inflammation. In AION, particularly the arteritic type, nerve-head enhancement has been reported more consistently than diffusion restriction.

document_sections.heading: Variant 6: Adult. Bitemporal hemianopia or junctional scotoma. Sellar or parasellar mass suspected. Initial imaging.
document_sections.content: Bitemporal hemianopia and junctional scotoma can arise from external compression or intrinsic disease of the optic chiasm and the optic nerve–chiasm junction, respectively. A pituitary macroadenoma may extend above the sella and compress the chiasm, adjacent nerves, or tracts. Meningiomas account for a small fraction of sellar-region masses but can involve sellar, suprasellar, or parasellar structures and compress the nerves or chiasm. Sellar or suprasellar meningiomas most often enhance homogeneously; a dural tail is common but not universal. Imaging cannot always distinguish them from a pituitary adenoma when their origin relative to the gland is uncertain. Craniopharyngiomas commonly compress the chiasm. The adamantinomatous type, more frequent in children, is often mixed cystic and solid, calcified, and heterogeneously enhancing; the adult papillary type is generally solid and enhancing and rarely calcifies. Hypophysitis, large Rathke cleft cysts, and other suprasellar masses may compress the chiasm or posterior optic nerves. Neoplastic causes usually produce gradual symptoms, whereas pituitary apoplexy, most often hemorrhagic infarction of an existing adenoma, can rapidly enlarge a lesion and cause headache and visual change. Large internal carotid artery or Circle of Willis aneurysms may also compress the visual pathway. Optic pathway glioma, inflammatory or demyelinating disease, granulomatous disease, and lymphoma may affect the chiasm, optic nerves, or pituitary infundibulum. Imaging aims to identify a sellar or suprasellar mass causing the field defect, demonstrate chiasmal compression, and guide care.

document_sections.heading: Arteriography Cerebral
document_sections.content: Relevant literature does not support initial cerebral arteriography for bitemporal hemianopia or junctional scotoma. Angiography may assist aneurysm treatment or pretreatment assessment of morphology and anatomy, but CTA or MRA are the initial examinations used to diagnose an aneurysm compressing the chiasm.

document_sections.heading: CT Sella With IV Contrast
document_sections.content: Relevant literature does not support its initial use. CT can demonstrate sellar or suprasellar mass and chiasmal compression, and complement MRI by identifying calcification or adjacent bone invasion; it is useful for masses arising from bone. MRI is preferred to characterize regional masses and intrinsic nerve or chiasmal disease because of superior soft-tissue resolution.

document_sections.heading: CT Sella Without IV Contrast
document_sections.content: Relevant literature does not support initial noncontrast sellar CT. CT can show a mass, chiasmal compression, calcification, adjacent bone invasion, and bone-origin lesions, but MRI better characterizes soft-tissue and visual-pathway disease. Noncontrast CT may reveal acute hemorrhagic hyperattenuation in pituitary apoplexy; MRI is more sensitive and can assess a previously undetected underlying pituitary mass.

document_sections.heading: CTA Head With IV Contrast
document_sections.content: A large internal carotid artery or Circle of Willis aneurysm can compress the chiasm or optic nerve–chiasm junction and cause visual symptoms. If initial MRI suggests an aneurysm, CTA or MRA subsequently establishes the diagnosis.

document_sections.heading: MRA Head With IV Contrast
document_sections.content: Relevant literature does not support its initial use for the visual-field presentation. When initial MRI suggests a compressive aneurysm, subsequent CTA or MRA establishes the diagnosis. Whether contrast is used for initial aneurysm diagnosis may depend on institutional preference. Contrast-enhanced MRA has compared favorably with DSA for assessing aneurysm dimensions and morphology.

document_sections.heading: MRA Head Without and With IV Contrast
document_sections.content: Relevant literature does not support its initial use for this presentation. Suspected compressive aneurysm on initial MRI is subsequently investigated by CTA or MRA, with contrast choice varying by institution. A large meta-analysis found high TOF MRA sensitivity for intracranial aneurysms >3 mm. TOF and contrast-enhanced MRA have similar aneurysm detection, but contrast-enhanced MRA more reliably depicts morphology.

document_sections.heading: MRA Head Without IV Contrast
document_sections.content: Relevant literature does not support its initial use for this presentation. After MRI suggests an aneurysm compressing the visual pathway, CTA or MRA can establish the diagnosis; contrast choice varies by institution. A large meta-analysis reported high TOF MRA sensitivity for aneurysms >3 mm. TOF and contrast-enhanced MRA detect aneurysms similarly, although contrast enhancement more reliably depicts morphology.

document_sections.heading: MRI Head Without and With IV Contrast
document_sections.content: Routine head MRI can generally diagnose a large pituitary macroadenoma compressing the chiasm. Compared with a dedicated sellar protocol, however, its sections are thicker and its coronal sequences vary by institution. Sellar MRI before and after contrast uses a smaller field, thinner images, and optimized sequences to provide better resolution and anatomic detail. Head MRI without and with IV contrast is useful for disease extending beyond the sella, including granulomatous disease, metastasis, and lymphoma.

document_sections.heading: MRI Sella Without and With IV Contrast
document_sections.content: Dedicated sellar MRI before and after IV contrast is the initial test of choice for suspected sellar or suprasellar disease causing bitemporal hemianopia or junctional scotoma. Thin coronal and sagittal precontrast and postcontrast T1-weighted images, together with T2-weighted images focused narrowly on the sella and suprasellar space, best depict the sellar and parasellar regions, cavernous sinuses, posterior optic nerves, and chiasm. The examination characterizes masses, inflammatory disease, and other regional conditions, their extent, and their relationship to the chiasm and cavernous sinus.

document_sections.heading: MRI Sella Without IV Contrast
document_sections.content: Relevant literature does not support noncontrast sellar MRI alone for initial imaging. It can depict a sellar or suprasellar mass and its relationship to the chiasm, but images before and after IV contrast best characterize disease extent and adjacent structures. Noncontrast MRI may show chiasmal T2 hyperintensity from inflammatory or demyelinating disease without distinguishing acute from chronic lesions.

document_sections.heading: Summary of Highlights
document_sections.content: Variant 1: Noncontrast orbital and maxillofacial CT are recommended alternative initial tests for traumatic orbital fractures or soft-tissue injury. The orbital field suits direct blunt or penetrating orbital trauma; the wider maxillofacial field suits possible additional facial injury. Add noncontrast head CT when traumatic brain injury or intracranial bleeding is suspected. Variant 2: Contrast-enhanced orbital or maxillofacial CT and orbital MRI without and with contrast are recommended initially. Emergency contrast-enhanced CT is first-line for disease extent and abscess; the CT choices are alternatives selected by the suspected field of involvement. Orbital MRI complements CT by better resolving soft tissues and separating abscess from phlegmon. Head MRI without and with contrast may be indicated for suspected intracranial spread. Variant 3: Orbital MRI without and with contrast is the test of choice for suspected orbital mass or vascular lesion. Head MRI may assess intracranial extension; contrast-enhanced orbital CT may complement MRI for calcification, bone involvement, or a primary osseous lesion. Variant 4: No imaging is indicated initially for a suspected retinal structural cause; ophthalmologic examination, potentially supported by ocular US, diagnoses detachment. Subsequently, contrast-enhanced orbital MRI may assess an underlying mass or other cause of exudative detachment. Variant 5: Orbital MRI without and with contrast is recommended initially for suspected optic nerve disease, while head MRI without and with contrast may complement it if associated intracranial disease is possible. Variant 6: Sellar MRI without and with contrast is recommended initially for suspected sellar or parasellar disease producing bitemporal hemianopia or junctional scotoma; head MRI may be indicated for processes extending beyond the sellar region, including granulomatous disease, metastasis, or lymphoma.

document_sections.heading: Appropriateness Category Names and Definitions
document_sections.content: The table defines Usually Appropriate as a rating of 7, 8, or 9 for an examination or treatment indicated in the specified setting with a favorable patient risk–benefit balance. May Be Appropriate corresponds to 4, 5, or 6 when an option might be indicated despite a more favorable alternative, or when the balance is uncertain. May Be Appropriate (Disagreement) receives 5 when individual panel ratings are too dispersed around the median; the label makes that disagreement visible. Usually Not Appropriate corresponds to 1, 2, or 3 when an option is unlikely to be indicated or its patient risk–benefit balance is likely unfavorable.

document_sections.heading: Relative Radiation Level Information
document_sections.content: Radiation-related health risk matters when choosing imaging. Relative Radiation Level, or RRL, conveys radiation exposure across procedures using effective dose, a measure for estimating population-level overall radiation risk. Pediatric patients have greater inherent exposure risk because of organ sensitivity and longer expected life, so pediatric dose ranges are lower than adult ranges. The table relates each RRL symbol to adult and pediatric effective-dose ranges: O corresponds to 0 mSv for both; ☢ to <0.1 mSv in adults and <0.03 mSv in children; ☢☢ to 0.1-1 mSv and 0.03-0.3 mSv; ☢☢☢ to 1-10 mSv and 0.3-3 mSv; ☢☢☢☢ to 10-30 mSv and 3-10 mSv; and ☢☢☢☢☢ to 30-100 mSv and 10-30 mSv, respectively. When patient dose depends too heavily on examination-specific factors to assign an RRL, the designation is “Varies.”
